theme: I was glad when they said, “Let us go to the house of the LORD”
readingInstruction: Read Psalm 122. It is a Song of Ascents of David, a joyful song for a pilgrim arriving in Jerusalem. Read it as a hope for the exiles, who longed to go up again.
settingTheScene: Psalm 122 is the third of the Songs of Ascents you have started reading. Pilgrims sang these as they climbed to Jerusalem for the festivals. For exiles in Babylon, it was a memory and a promise: someday they would stand in those gates again. The psalm is about three things: the joy of going to the house of the LORD, the city as a place of unity and justice, and the prayer for its peace.
observation: “I was glad when they said to me, Let us go to the house of the LORD!” (v. 1).
“Our feet have been standing within your gates, O Jerusalem!” (v. 2).
“Jerusalem, built as a city that is bound firmly together” (v. 3).
“To which the tribes go up, the tribes of the LORD, as was decreed for Israel, to give thanks to the name of the LORD” (v. 4).
“There thrones for judgment were set, the thrones of the house of David” (v. 5).
“Pray for the peace of Jerusalem! May they be secure who love you!” (v. 6).
“Peace be within your walls and security within your towers!” (v. 7).
“For the sake of the house of the LORD our God, I will seek your good” (v. 9).
interpretation:
The psalm opens with gladness. The psalmist was glad when others said, “Let us go.” It is a statement about the joy of communal worship. We do not usually travel alone to God’s house. Someone invites us, and we go together. And he remembers the first words: “Let us go.” There is something about being invited into worship that stirs the heart.

The second verse is the arrival. “Our feet have been standing within your gates.” The journey is over, and they are in the city. For the exiles, this verse must have been bittersweet. They had no gates to stand in. But they could dream of it, and the psalm gave them words.

Jerusalem is described as a city “bound firmly together,” a place of unity. The tribes go up together to give thanks, and justice is administered there. The city is the center of the covenant community. It is a picture of what God’s people are meant to be: united, worshiping, and just.

The psalm ends with a prayer for peace. “Pray for the peace of Jerusalem!” There is a word play on the city’s name, which means “foundation of peace.” The peace prayed for is shalom, wholeness and well-being, within the walls and in the towers. And the motive is love: “For the sake of my brothers and companions, I will say, Peace be within you!” And the highest reason: “For the sake of the house of the LORD our God, I will seek your good.”

For Christians, Jerusalem is not just a geographic place. The church is described as the new Jerusalem, the “Jerusalem above.” This psalm teaches us to love the gathered people of God, to take joy in worship, and to pray for the church’s peace and unity.
connection: Hebrews 12:22-24 says that believers have come to Mount Zion, “the heavenly Jerusalem.” Galatians 4:26 speaks of “the Jerusalem above” as our mother. Revelation 21:2 describes the new Jerusalem coming down from heaven like a bride. Hebrews 10:24-25 calls us not to neglect meeting together. Ephesians 4:3 urges us to maintain the unity of the Spirit in the bond of peace. John 14:27: “Peace I leave with you; my peace I give to you.”
application:
Be glad in going to church this week. Pray ahead of time for those you will meet.

Pray for the peace and unity of your own church by name, as the psalm prays for Jerusalem.

Invite someone to worship with you, as in verse 1: “Let us go to the house of the LORD.”
prayerPrompts: Tell God you are glad to go to his house.
Ask him to bind his church together in peace.
Pray for your own church by name.
